newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military sees no move by Iraq against Kurds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military sees no move by Iraq against Kurds.

text.p: U.S. defence officials said on Monday they had no indication that Iraq's military might be preparing to attack Kurds in northern Iraq.

The officials were asked about a statement by an Iraqi Kurdish group, which said in Turkey that it was worried about movements of Iraqi armour and a possible attack on Kurdish territory in a row over the supply of water from Kurdish-controlled northern Iraq.

"We haven't seen a (military) build-up or anything that would indicate that there is any imminent threat of attack" against the Kurds, Navy Capt. Mark Neuharth, a spokesman for the U.S. military's Central Command in Tampa, told Reuters.
The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) said in a statement earlier that it was concerned over what it called recent deployments of Iraqi armour in the area of Kifri, south of Darbandikhan.
The opposition Iraqi National Congress (INC) also said in a statement on Monday that heavily armed government forces were massing around the town of Kifri, 100 miles (160 km) northeast of Baghdad.

The PUK rejected accusations made by Baghdad last week that it was cutting the water flow from Dokan and Darbandikhan dams in northern Iraq, outside government control since the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait.
The PUK said it feared that Iraqi government of President Saddam Hussein might use the complaint as a pretext for an attack against the Kurds.

Baghdad has said the cutoff from the dams has caused severe shortages in Diyala (Ba'quba) province, 37 miles (60 km) northeast of Baghdad and the oil-rich Ta'meem (Kirkuk) province, 175 miles (280 km) north of Baghdad.

Iraqi forces last September helped the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) led by Massoud Barzani oust rival rebels of the PUK from the city of Arbil. The move prompted the United States to fire missiles against Iraqi air defences in the south.
